newsitem.title: EGYPT: Officials tout investment reform at Mideast meeting.
newsitem.headline: Officials tout investment reform at Mideast meeting.

text.p: Middle Eastern and North African countries need to overhaul investment and trade laws to foster regional integration and foreign investment, a top U.S. trade official said on Tuesday.
Stuart Eizenstat, U.S. Undersecretary of Commerce for International Trade, said the pursuit of peace alone would not be enough to attract investors and boost intra-regional trade.
"There is vast potential in the region," he said at the Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference.
"The question is will we see the Middle East have the same kind of take-off that Asia and Latin America have experienced over the past several years."
Eizenstat said some Middle Eastern countries needed a clear commercial code, deregulation, lower tariffs, legal predictability and more privatisation.
Barriers including the boycott of Israel, differing standards and conflicting regulations were "inhibiting integration".

"The countries in the Middle East have demonstrated progress in many of these areas. Once these reforms continue to take root increased foreign investment and jobs will surely follow. Peace may be one of the preconditions for prosperity," he said.
The three-day conference which started on Tuesday has focused partly on how peace between Israel and Arabs could help encourage foreign investment and prosperity.

But economists and officials at the meeting said MENA region countries needed to get their own houses in order. They cited insufficient intellectual property laws, legal uncertainties and high duties.

Intra-regional trade is limited to about seven percent of the total trade of Middle Eastern and North African countries, Eizenstat said, compared with more than 60 percent in the European Union and more than 30 percent in Asia.
He said this could be improved with a "continued political commitment to peace" and "integrated commercial arrangements".
Makboul bin Ali bin Sultan, Oman's commerce and industry minister, said export and investment information was lacking.

Nemat Shafik, the World Bank's manager for the Middle East and North Africa private sector, said non-oil exports in the region of 250 million people "have been incredibly low," or about the same as Finland, which has some six million people.
She said per capita average exports were $100 in MENA compared with $3,000 in South East Asia.

"Export growth in the MENA region has lagged but several countries have made important strides and I think we may be on the verge of a turning point," Shafik said in a speech. "Clearly there is an enormous need to increase the non-oil exports."
Shafik said better private exporter incentives were needed. "I would go to zero tariffs as fast as I could," she said.
